deviations.external_standard_requirement: V11.6.1: only approved cryptographic algorithms and modes for key generation and seeding, and digital signature generation and verification.
deviations.conflicting_requirement: Appendix C Digital Signatures approves EdDSA (Ed25519, Ed448), XEdDSA, ECDSA (P-256, P-384, P-521), RSA-PSS; ECDSA over secp256k1 is not listed. Appendix C also states: "This list may be overridden in the context of a given application for various reasons including: new evolutions in the field of cryptography; compliance with regulation."
required_protocol_source: SRC-ERC4361 §Signing and Verifying Messages with Ethereum Accounts
deviations.required_protocol_requirement: ERC-4361: "For Externally Owned Accounts (EOAs), the verification method specified in ERC-191 MUST be used." ERC-191 verification recovers the signer with ecrecover. Yellow Paper Appendix F: "Transactions are signed using recoverable ECDSA signatures. This method utilises the SECP-256k1 curve"; an Ethereum address is the rightmost 160 bits of the Keccak-256 hash of that ECDSA public key; ECREC = ECDSARECOVER over secp256k1n.
deviations.reason: An EOA is defined by a secp256k1 key pair. Proving control of an EOA (the purpose of SIWE login and wallet linking) is only possible by verifying a secp256k1 ECDSA signature. CoverRaccoon does not choose the curve; the wallet and the Ethereum protocol do.
deviations.security_impact: No standalone weakness demonstrated. secp256k1 gives ~128-bit security (V11.2.3 satisfied by CR-CRYPTO-005); it is not a NIST/FIPS curve, and no practical attack against it is known.
deviations.risk_assessment: Conformance-level deviation, low residual risk: (1) future cryptanalysis of secp256k1, shared with the whole Ethereum ecosystem; (2) no crypto agility for EOA verification (tracked separately by CR-CRYPTO-004, not hidden here); (3) signature malleability: the recovery stack accepts the high-s twin of a valid signature (Q-CRYPTO-LOW-S, EV-PROBE-LOW-S); no impact found because a malleated signature recovers the same signer, signatures are never stored or used as identifiers, and every challenge is single-use (CR-CONC-001).
mitigations: verification only through viem 2.55.13 -> @noble/curves 1.9.1 (no custom curve arithmetic), lockfile-pinned with integrity hashes and CI registry-signature verification (CR-SUPPLY-001/004)
field checks (domain, uri, chain-id, nonce, times, address) before any signature check (CR-AUTH-001)
exact 65-byte EOA signature format checked before recovery
contract wallets verified by the wallet contract via ERC-1271 with two providers at one block (CR-AUTH-003)
alternatives_considered: ECDSA P-256 / EdDSA for EOA login: impossible, EOA keys are secp256k1 and wallets cannot sign for that account with another curve
EIP-712 typed-data signatures: same curve and hash, no change in conformance
P-256 (passkey) smart accounts via ERC-1271 / P256VERIFY: possible for some contract wallets, cannot be required of users, and verification happens in the contract, not in CoverRaccoon
non-wallet authentication: removes the required functionality (proof of wallet ownership)
deviations.why_alternatives_not_viable: Every standards-conformant alternative either cannot verify control of an existing Ethereum EOA or excludes EOA users, which breaks the product function (monitoring and protecting a user's own wallet).
implementation_constraints: EOA address derivation and signature scheme fixed by the Ethereum protocol
wallet software determines the signing scheme
SIWE (ERC-4361) mandates ERC-191 verification for EOAs

evidence_questions.question: Does the current ECDSA recovery stack enforce or normalise low-s signatures?
evidence_questions.answer: No. viem 2.55.13 verifyMessage -> @noble/curves 1.9.1 recovery accepts the high-s twin (n - s, flipped v) of a valid signature for the same address (EV-PROBE-LOW-S, reproducible).
evidence_questions.impact_classification: INFORMATIONAL - not an authentication bypass: the twin proves the same key; replay protection is the single-use server nonce, not signature uniqueness; signatures are never persisted or used as keys (source search 2026-10-16).
evidence_questions.review_if: signatures are ever stored, deduplicated or used as identifiers

external_standard_source: SRC-ASVS-APPC §Hash Functions for General Use Cases
deviations.external_standard_requirement: V11.4.1: only approved hash functions for general cryptographic use cases, including digital signatures, HMAC, KDF and random bit generation; disallowed hashes such as MD5 must not be used.
deviations.conflicting_requirement: Appendix C approves SHA3-512/384/256, SHA-512/384/256, SHA-512/256, SHAKE256, BLAKE2s/b, BLAKE3 for digital signatures; Keccak-256 (original Keccak padding, not FIPS 202) is not listed. It is not listed as Disallowed either.
required_protocol_source: SRC-ERC4361 §Signing and Verifying Messages with Ethereum Accounts
SRC-ERC191 (version 0x45 personal_sign; verification example keccak256 + ecrecover)
SRC-ETH-YP §Conventions KEC, Appendix E ECREC, Appendix F
deviations.required_protocol_requirement: Wallets sign keccak256("\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n" + len + message) (ERC-191 personal_sign); ecrecover and ERC-1271 isValidSignature take that 32-byte digest. The Yellow Paper defines KEC as "the Keccak-256 hash function (... rather than the final SHA-3 specification)".
deviations.reason: The digest under a wallet signature is fixed by the wallet and the protocol. A verifier that hashes with SHA3-256 instead would never match the signature the wallet produced.
deviations.security_impact: No standalone weakness demonstrated. Keccak-256 differs from SHA3-256 only in domain-separation padding and offers the same 256-bit output and 128-bit collision resistance.
deviations.risk_assessment: Conformance-level deviation, low residual risk: (1) future cryptanalysis of Keccak, shared with SHA-3 and Ethereum; (2) scope creep: Keccak must not spread to application-chosen hashing (guarded by CR-CRYPTO-007 and CR-CRYPTO-009 P4).
mitigations: application-chosen hashing is SHA-256 / HMAC-SHA-256 only (CR-CRYPTO-007)
lockfile integrity and registry-signature verification for the hashing library (CR-SUPPLY-001/004)
alternatives_considered: SHA3-256 / SHA-256 digest for SIWE: wallets do not produce such signatures; verification would always fail
deviations.why_alternatives_not_viable: The hash is part of the signed-data format; changing it breaks interoperability with every Ethereum wallet and with ERC-1271 contracts.
implementation_constraints: ecrecover and ERC-1271 operate on Keccak-256 digests

deviations.external_standard_requirement: V4.1.2: only user-facing endpoints automatically redirect from HTTP to HTTPS; other services or endpoints do not implement transparent redirects.
deviations.conflicting_requirement: http://coverraccoon.com/api/* is answered with 308 to https by the Vercel edge (observed 2026-10-16).
deviations.required_protocol_requirement: Vercel: "HTTPS redirection is an industry standard and can't be disabled."
deviations.reason: The redirect is issued by the hosting edge before any application code runs; Vercel offers no project setting to refuse HTTP instead.
deviations.security_impact: A client that erroneously sends an API request over HTTP leaks that request in clear text and the redirect hides the mistake.
deviations.risk_assessment: Low and bounded: the only intended API client is the same-origin HTTPS frontend (relative fetches; mixed content is blocked); HSTS max-age 1 year with includeSubDomains on all hosts; session cookies are Secure and __Host- (never sent over HTTP); Bearer credentials are never accepted; Telegram setWebhook only accepts HTTPS URLs; Vercel Cron calls are platform-internal. Residual: domain not on the HSTS preload list, so a first-contact browser can still send one HTTP navigation (not an API request with credentials).
deviations.trust_assumption: Vercel edge behaves as documented: every HTTP request is answered with a redirect to the same host and path over HTTPS, before reaching functions.
alternatives_considered: refuse HTTP for /api in application code: impossible, the edge redirects before functions run
Vercel setting to disable the redirect: does not exist per SRC-VERCEL-ENC
serve the API from a host that refuses HTTP: changes the hosting platform; not an application-level configuration
HSTS preload: reduces first-contact exposure but does not remove the redirect
deviations.why_alternatives_not_viable: No application-level or project-level configuration can make the edge refuse HTTP; the only conformant option is a platform migration, disproportionate to a bounded conformance-level exposure.
implementation_constraints: Vercel edge terminates TLS and owns HTTP handling
